topComments.text: Use zswap not zram if you have a backing device: https://linuxblog.io/zswap-better-than-zram/ https://chrisdown.name/2026/03/24/zswap-vs-zram-when-to-use-...

topComments.author: mzhaase
topComments.text: Zram vs Zswap: https://chrisdown.name/2026/03/24/zswap-vs-zram-when-to-use-... > If in doubt, prefer to use zswap. Only use zram if you have a highly specific reason to. > In terms of architecture: > zswap sits in front of your disk swap, compresses pages in RAM, and automatically tiers cold data to disk. It integrates directly with the kernel's memory management and distributes pressure gracefully. > zram is a compressed RAM block device with a hard capacity limit. When you put swap on it and it fills up, there is no automatic eviction, and the kernel has very little leverage to do anything about the situation. The system either OOMs or falls back to lower-priority swap, causing LRU inversion (see below). It only really makes sense for extremely memory-constrained embedded systems, diskless setups, or cases with specific security requirements around keeping private data off persistent storage. Swap on zram is also increasingly unsupported upstream.

topComments.author: jkingsman
topComments.text: Even dumber local models that are heavily quantized to fit on consumer GPUs can be lovely as a dimwitted household assistant. A lot of people look to offload things they already do to LLMs, which can be great with frontier models, but you've got the highest standards and preferences for tasks you already do, so it's the most likely to fall into a "should have just done that myself" outcome. I've found great success in instead lowering my threshold of things I'd take time to do -- I wouldn't spend time on it, but I'd spend 60s prompting an LLM to take a crack. I'm fortunate to have the hardware to run Qwen 3.8 Flash Next at q8, but most of the tasks I have it do would be totally doable for a mid-quant Qwen 3.8 27b. Some recent tasks I've thrown it: * Go through my blood test data (from EHR XML dumps from prior years) and give me some over-time charts for consistently-sampled measurements * Go through my Good Articles bookmarks, epubify them, and drop one down onto my ereader each morning for my commute, then archive the offline version into cold storage * Go through my music library, identify my most-listened low-bitrate tracks, and source or assemble a shopping cart to get high res versions * Analyze local tax/foreclosure auctions for vacant land; grab aerial screenshots, tax data, ownership data, and compile a weekly report of things maybe worth bidding on based on some specific selection criteria (fun facts: if you're willing to accept some headaches, 5+ acres can be yours for under $5k, if you're in the right area) * Dump my grocery store loyalty data, analyze my purchasing habits, and prepare a weekly instacart for my approval that aims to sync with usage habits. Tweak and learn volume/order adjustments over time. * Given a KVM that can mount ISOs onto the host, reimage two old laptops of unknown status with Debian and install Minecraft so my nieces and I can have a LAN party * Organize my music (high confidence MusicBrainz Picard matches), movies/TV shows, ebooks, and video game ROM collections with metadata and good folder organization * Archive bookmarked fanfiction for my offline library (slowly, and respectfully, and with an actual browser. The browser is anti-bot-countermeasured to the gills, but QFN regularly solves hCaptcha and Cloudflare turnstile challenges. Once I gave it the ability to drag, it even reasonably reliably solves drag-shape captchas. A little while back it made a purchase on eBay which is NOT a bot friendly site.) Would I personally spend time on doing most of these? Generally not. Could an LLM screw them up so badly I regret it? Also generally not. I get the luxury of a psuedo-assistant that doesn't judge how menial the tasks I send it are, and I save time. With a local LLM, my privacy concerns are far less than with frontier models, and local abliterated models are less (or just not at all) twitchy around things that frontier classifiers balk at. I'm hopeful that big projects like Muse can help to normalize menial task offloading, and that local LLMs provide the bridge for more technically minded folks to use them even more aggressively and limitlessly (as in compute limits/subscription costs) and cheaply.

stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: In an alarm dashboard, an operator can select one device or show all devices. I am testing the all-device branch in the table dialect on Apache IoTDB 2.0.11. The minimal setup and failing operation are: CREATE DATABASE alarm_console; USE alarm_console; CREATE TABLE alerts(device STRING TAG,severity INT32 FIELD); INSERT INTO alerts(time,device,severity) VALUES(1000,'pump_a',1),(2000,'pump_b',2); USE alarm_console; SELECT device,severity FROM alerts WHERE ('all'='all' OR device='pump_a') ORDER BY time; Observed result: Msg: The statement is executed successfully. Msg: org.apache.iotdb.jdbc.IoTDBSQLException: 305: [INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR(305)] Exception occurred: "SELECT device,severity FROM alerts WHERE ('all'='all' OR device='pump_a') ORDER BY time". executeStatement failed. Both object must be type of number For comparison, a numeric constant branch keeps both rows: USE alarm_console; SELECT device,severity FROM alerts WHERE 1=1 OR device='pump_a' ORDER BY time; +------+--------+ |device|severity| +------+--------+ |pump_a| 1| |pump_b| 2| +------+--------+ Filtering by the device tag works as expected: USE alarm_console; SELECT device,severity FROM alerts WHERE device='pump_a' ORDER BY time; +------+--------+ |device|severity| +------+--------+ |pump_a| 1| +------+--------+ The string IN form also keeps both rows: USE alarm_console; SELECT device,severity FROM alerts WHERE 'all' IN ('all') OR device='pump_a' ORDER BY time; +------+--------+ |device|severity| +------+--------+ |pump_a| 1| |pump_b| 2| +------+--------+ The table dialect allows STRING-to-STRING comparisons, so I expected the constant expression to be true and both devices to remain in the result. "Coexistence" can sync one-to-one chats for a WhatsApp Business app number, but group chats are not synced. - The Groups API only seems to cover groups created by an Official Business Account (max 8 participants). - Automating WhatsApp Web (Puppeteer, whatsapp-web.js, Baileys) or decrypting backups appears to violate WhatsApp's Terms of Service, which prohibit accessing or collecting data "through automated means", so I've ruled these out. The deployment also lowered compute costs by 10%, improved application runtimes by 14%, and reduced shuffle costs per task by nearly 90% through dedicated storage, replication, and data-plane optimizations. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Behind Booking.com's AI Evolution: The Unpolished Story
infoqArticles.description: Jabez Eliezer Manuel discusses the 20-year evolution of Booking.com’s data management and ML platforms. He explains how they scaled MySQL topologies, sunset Hadoop for cloud architecture, and built high-throughput model serving and feature stores operating at 400B predictions per day. He also shares insights on personalization, interleaved experimentation, and their new agentic AI foundation. By J
infoqArticles.author: Jabez Eliezer Manuel

infoqArticles.title: Vercel Releases UI SDK for Agents to Compose UI from Reusable Behaviors
infoqArticles.description: Vercel has released UI SDK in beta, an Apache 2.0 TypeScript library of more than 50 UI behaviors in @ui-sdk/core, with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components, so agents can compose accessible components and operate them through a documented agent bridge. By Daniel Dominguez
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Dominguez

infoqArticles.title: AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account
infoqArticles.description: AWS has detailed tunnel endpoints, a PrivateLink endpoint type that gives a consumer VPC access to an entire network segment in another account rather than one resource at a time, over an overlapping address space and with consumer-initiated connections only. The consumer must wrap traffic in GENEVE; only TCP and DNS pass, and access logs cannot attribute traffic to a workload behind the endpoint.
infoqArticles.author: Steef-Jan Wiggers

infoqArticles.title: Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes
infoqArticles.description: Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at new pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. By Claudio Masolo
infoqArticles.author: Claudio Masolo

infoqArticles.title: How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development without Overloading Developers' Machines
infoqArticles.description: To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: Qwik 2.0 RC: Replaces HTML Comment Markers for Faster Reactivity and Out-of-Order Streaming
infoqArticles.description: Qwik 2.0 Release Candidate, published on 1 October 2026, replaces v1's HTML comment markers with two script blocks that hold state and virtual node data. It adds experimental out-of-order streaming, async useComputed$, and cacheable route loaders. Qwik's benchmarks show v2 at 1.23x vanilla JavaScript, versus 2.59x for v1. A migration command is provided. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability
